commonValues: Sawfishes (Family Pristidae, a family of batoid fishes) may be confused with sawsharks (Family Pristiophoridae) in having a rostral saw but differ from sawsharks in having the pectoral fins expanded anteriorly over gill slits and fused to sides of head, so that head and pectoral fins form a distinct pectoral disc with the gill slits ventral. The trunk is shorter and more depressed, first dorsal fins partially or entirely above pelvic-fin bases, rostral saw has uniformly large, relatively few, continuously growing teeth, and no barbels.  Sawfishes are also generally larger (6m or more) than sawsharks (less than 2m) (Ref. 9859; 31368).

Wobbegongs (Family Orectolobidae) is similar with angelsharks  (Family Squatinidae) in having considerably depressed bodies but the pectoral fins are much smaller and anal fin is absent. Their distinctive flattened body and the narrow dermal flaps of skin around mouth and head distinguish wobbegongs from other shark families (Ref. 13577, 31369).
Has a slender and lateral line, and predorsal scales (Ref. 10294).

Young with dark grey-brown bands outlined in black (Ref. 13575, 43278). commonValues: Eggs have thin, transparent, purplish-blue chorion (Ref. 109195).

Each embryo is surrounded by the following membranes: the egg covering, egg capsule, coiled capsule tube, and the external limiting membrane which is layered, the outer layer being somewhat fibrous in nature, the inner resembling the coiled capsule tube. Each capsule is provided with an oval trap-doorlike structure, which is a means of escape for the veliger at hatching (Ref. 105320).

Yolky egg.  Egg color is green (Ref. 105349).  Eight hours after fertilization, the prototroch was well-developed, an apical tuft present and the cilia were beating.  Green-pigmented dots were restricted to the area above the prototroch, while the turquoise area was below.  By 8 to 9 hrs , the trochophore was spinning within the egg membrane in an irregular manner. Polar bodies were visible within the egg membrane until hatching occurred.
Eggs range from light purple or burgundy, becoming dark purple and purple-brown in color.
Egg jelly completely transparent and egg chorion swells as embryo develops reaching a diameter of about 0.2 cm during hatching.

commonValues: Hatching occurred between 9 and 11 hrs after fertilization at the trochophore stage.  The earliest occurred before the shell could be discerned, while some larvae hatched with a small shell cap already formed, covering about two-thirds to three-fourths ofthe posterior end ofthe larvae, with a slight bulging of propodium.  The larval shell was transparent white, marked with irregular, broken spiral striations. Larvae were active swimmers, with much vertical movement.

commonValues: Larvae were found at 100 to 400 m.

The pre-torsional veliger, with a well-developed velum, was noted between 17 and 22 hrs after fertilization.  The propodium was large, and the larval shell had a distinct whorl.  The velum was round and single-lobed, resembling that of a bivalve veliger.  As the velum developed, the green pigment aggregated around the outside of the velum in large, elliptical spots with the smaller dots still present in the prevelar area.  The turquoise pigment was concentrated in the digestive gland area and indicated the larva's yolk supply. At 23 to 26 hrs after fertilization the larval shell was complete, having one complete whorl, measuring 0.27 to 0.28 mm at its greatest width.  The operculum was well-formed, the mantle cavity evident and the larva could withdraw completely into the shell.  Two tiny black eye spots were apparent on the prevelar area, and torsion was complete.  The velum of the veliger gradually became bilobed between 24 to 48 hrs after fertilization and was accentuated by two rings of green chromatophores, but it remained small.  The eye spots became larger and more distinct, and the foot became noticeably larger.  Between 48 and 72 hrs after fertilization, the velum had distinct, dark green "rims" on the outer side of each lobe, and small protuberances of the tentacles were evident near the eye spots.  The lecithotrophic larvae search for the substratum with their foot, now ciliated, outstretched.  Sixty hours after fertilization, many larvae were crawling, with the twirling velum protruding from beneath the larval shell opening. Larvae altemated between swimming and crawling during this
period.  At about 3 days, the foot became very sticky, and the larvae could attach quickly to a substratum.

Tentaculate-stage:  from hatching until approximatley 4 mm in length; feeds using tentacles .  Transition-stage:  body length approximately 5 mm; begin to develop small oral lobes; tentacles resorbed into tentacle bulbs and gradually disappear; feeds by tentaculate and lobate mechanism. Lobate-stage:   approximately 6 mm; tentacles completely reduced; auricles develop. Post-larvae:  approximately 14 to 15 mm; lobes and auricles completely developed (Ref. 1106).
Paralarvae are planktonic (as are early juveniles), becomes demersal 15-30 days after.

Polyp stage:  Potentially perennial polyps, 0.1 to 0.3 cm high, goblet-shaped, with about 16 filiform tentacles.  Mouth cruciform, oral disc with about four peristomal pits.  Possess 2 types of nematocysts, atrichous isorhizas and microbasic heterotrichous euryteles.
Ephyra stage:  Ephyra with 8 pairs of lappets and 8 rhopalia, lappets slender and distally pointed.  Rhopalar clefts deeply cut, reaching over half-way along ephyral arms.  Manubrium short and quadrate.  Gastrovascular cavity with 16 broad radial pouches.

commonValues: This species is a non-broadcast spawner.  Life cycle does not include trocophore stage.  Also Ref. 833.

Members of the class Insecta are gonochoric; sperm transfer is usually direct with copulation (presence of a penis) but may also be indirect (via spermatophores).  Life cycle:  egg develops into a juvenile and later into an adult through molting.

Members of the order Isopoda are mostly gonochoric.  Mating behavior:  Mating usually occurs before and sometimes during the parturial molt.  Sperm transfer is indirect.  Life cycle:  Eggs are brooded in the marsupium, which later hatch into manca postlarva before developing into adults.

Members of the class Bivalvia are mostly gonochoric, some are protandric hermaphrodites.  Life cycle:  Embryos develop into free-swimming trocophore larvae, succeeded by the bivalve veliger, resembling a miniature clam.

Members of the class Polychaeta are mostly gonochoric (sexual).  Mating:  Females produce a pheromone attracting and signalling the males to shed sperm which in turn stimulates females to shed eggs, this behavior is known as swarming.  Gametes are spawned through the metanephridia or body wall rupturing (termed as "epitoky", wherein a pelagic, reproductive individual, "epitoke", is formed from a benthic, nonreproductive individual, "atoke").  After fertilization, most eggs become planktonic; although some are retained in the worm tubes or burrowed in jelly masses attached to the tubes (egg brooders).  Life Cycle:  Eggs develop into trocophore larva, which later metamorph into juvenile stage (body lengthened), and later develop into adults.
